To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

1) LTP in the hippocampus is accompanied by changes in the activity of remote brain regions, including the neocortex and amygdala, 2) these changes are not due to a general change in brain state, and 3) LTP-induced changes in brain activity are not due to the direct stimulation of these remote regions.
LTP induces changes in brain activity that are not restricted to local changes in synaptic strength but also involve widespread, remote brain areas, including the contralateral hemisphere.
LTP in the hippocampus is associated with increased interhemispherical communication and recruitment of neocortical and limbic regions.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the functional and structural plasticity of the hippocampus
the mechanisms by which the brain changes its activity and function in response to environmental stimuli.
the neural mechanisms of memory and learning, and how they are affected by aging and Alzheimer's disease.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the LTP induced by microstimulation of the hippocampus leads to an increase of the functional connectivity of the hippocampus with the rest of the brain.
LTP induces network reorganization that involves increased interhemispherical communication and recruitment of neocortical and limbic areas, and that these changes can be measured using fMRI.
LTP-induced network changes are not restricted to the hippocampus and are not necessarily limited to the hippocampal formation.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
LTP-induced plasticity in the hippocampus leads to a global reorganization of brain networks that is detectable using fMRI.
LTP-induced changes in hippocampal synaptic strength are accompanied by a global change in brain activity.
LTP induces network reorganization in the brain that may underlie the behavioral changes that are seen with learning.
The main takeaway from our work is that
LTP-induced changes in the hippocampal formation are not restricted to local synaptic modifications, but rather they are part of a widespread network reorganization.
LTP is a global process that affects the entire brain, and not a local event that only affects the synapse that was stimulated.
LTP, the most prominent model of learning, can be used to study brain plasticity and network reorganization.
